Occupational performance, protective Objectives: To validate an adapted version of the Assessment of Work shelter, mental health disability, allied Performance (AWP) for use in Thai homeless shelters and to identify functional health, functional assessment. skill patterns and psychosocial barriers that inform allied health service planning. Materials and methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted with 60 adults with mental health–related disabilities residing in a government-operated destitute shelter. Participants completed a work-based AWP task rated across seven subskills. Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) examined the underlying factor structure, while regression analysis tested the predictive value of extracted factors on occupational performance. Results: The EFA supported a two-factor solution; 1) task adaptation and relational organization, and 2) communication and expression-accounting for 56.78% of the total variance (KMO=0.696, Bartlett’s test significant). Regression analysis showed that task adaptation and relational organization significantly predicted occupational performance, explaining 69.6% of the variance (R²=0.696). Conclusion: Task adaptation and environmental structuring are key deter- minants of occupational engagement in institutional shelter settings. Perfor- mance-based assessment, combined with structured observation during task engagement, provides a culturally relevant strategy for allied health profes- sionals to guide individualized rehabilitation for marginalized populations in Thai homeless shelters. JSON: Name: thai_shelter_awp_efa Title: Exploratory factor analysis of an adapted Assessment of Work Performance to identify functional determinants of occupational engagement in Thai homeless shelters Short Hypothesis: Among adults with mental health–related disabilities residing in Thai homeless shelters, higher scores on task adaptation and relational organization cause higher total occupational performance (AWP_TOTAL) after controlling for cognitive function (RUDAS) and psychiatric symptom severity (BPRS). Related Work: Performance-based assessments (e.g., Assessment of Work Performance, Executive Function Performance Test) have been used to evaluate motor, process, and communication-interaction skills relevant to functional engagement. Prior validation work supports construct validity and clinical utility in vocational and rehabilitation contexts, but existing studies have limitations: samples are often clinical or community-based rather than institutionalized homeless shelter residents; instruments are rarely adapted for local cultural and task repertoires; psychometric evaluations tend to rely on small samples and exploratory analyses without subsequent confirmatory testing; and the influence of psychiatric symptom severity and cognitive status on factor structure and predictive validity is inconsistently addressed. There is limited evidence on how task adaptation and environmental structuring operate as latent constructs in shelter settings and limited cross-site generalizability or longitudinal data on stability of identified factors. Abstract: Problem: Institutional homeless shelters constrain everyday occupations for adults with mental health–related disabilities and there is a lack of culturally adapted, performance-based tools to identify functional skill domains that predict occupational engagement. Approach: Adapt the Assessment of Work Performance (AWP) to shelter-relevant tasks and apply rigorous factor-analytic and predictive modeling to identify latent skill domains and quantify their contribution to overall occupational performance while accounting for cognitive status and psychiatric symptom severity. Main contribution: A validated, context-adapted factor structure of the AWP for Thai homeless shelters and quantified predictive models that isolate the effect size of task adaptation and relational organization on occupational outcomes. Expected outcome: Identification of 1–2 robust, replicable functional factors that explain a majority of variance in performance metrics, providing actionable assessment targets for allied health planning in institutional shelter settings. Experiments: 1) Datasets: (a) Pilot dataset: existing sample of 60 adults from one government-operated shelter (use for preliminary EFA); (b) Primary dataset: multi-site sample N=200 adults with mental health–related disabilities recruited from 3 government-operated Thai homeless shelters; inclusion: age 18–64, documented mental disorder, clinically stable without acute psychosis, Thai fluency, ability to perform basic self-care; exclusion: neurological disorders preventing task participation, severe sensory impairment. Collect AWP-adapted task ratings (7 subskills), RUDAS, BPRS, demographic and length-of-stay data. Obtain test–retest subsample N=50 at 2-week interval and interrater subsample N=50 with independent raters. 2) Baselines: (a) original non-adapted AWP factor structure (published model), (b) full AWP item set (if available), (c) no-factor univariate models using raw subskill sums, (d) EFPT-derived process scores (where feasible). 3) Analysis pipeline: (a) Split primary dataset into EFA sample (n=120) and CFA sample (n=80); (b) On EFA sample perform principal axis factoring with oblique rotation, determine factors via parallel analysis and MAP; report KMO, Bartlett's test, communalities, factor loadings; (c) On CFA sample fit competing models (one-factor, two-factor, original published structure) using SEM, report RMSEA, CFI, TLI, SRMR, χ2, AIC, BIC; (d) Evaluate internal consistency (Cronbach's α, McDonald's ω), test–retest ICC, and interrater ICC; (e) Predictive modeling: multiple linear regression and regularized regression (LASSO) predicting AWP_TOTAL from factor scores controlling for RUDAS, BPRS, age, sex, length of stay; report R2, adjusted R2, β coefficients, p-values, and bootstrapped 95% CIs; (f) Cross-validated prediction: 10-fold CV on primary dataset to estimate out-of-sample R2 and RMSE. 4) Ablations and comparisons: (a) Ablation A: remove task adaptation items and re-run CFA/regression to measure drop in explained variance; (b) Ablation B: compare adapted 7-item AWP vs expanded task set (if available) on fit and predictive power; (c) Sensitivity: repeat analyses stratified by shelter site, sex, and cognitive status (RUDAS above/below median). 5) Statistical thresholds: two-sided α=0.05 with correction for multiple model comparisons (Benjamini-Hochberg). 6) Reporting: report standardized effect sizes, model diagnostics, and residual analyses. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Sample size and power: factor analysis and CFA require adequate sample sizes; multi-site recruitment may still yield insufficient numbers per estimated parameter leading to unstable solutions. 2) Measurement bias: observer-rated AWP may suffer rater drift, halo effects, and interrater variability; test–retest intervals may reflect practice or mood effects. 3) Restricted variance and ceiling/floor effects: institutional tasks or simplified adaptations may produce reduced variability and attenuated correlations. 4) Confounding and causality: cross-sectional design limits causal inference; psychiatric symptom fluctuations or medication effects can confound associations. 5) Generalizability: findings may not transfer to non-institutional homeless populations, other cultural contexts, or shelters with different routines. 6) Translation and cultural validity: linguistic or conceptual mismatches in the adapted AWP may bias item interpretation. 7) Missing data and selection bias: exclusion of acutely symptomatic residents and reliance on stable long-term residents may bias results toward higher functioning profiles. 8) Statistical assumptions: violations of normality, multicollinearity among items, or measurement invariance across sites may invalidate SEM/CFA results. 9) Ethical constraints: vulnerable population requires strict consent protocols that may limit sample representativeness. 10) Computational limitations: none substantial for analyses described, but complex SEM with small samples may produce nonconvergent models.
